opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I don't hold any grudge about it at all. I think it was a completely reasonable decision from their side. At that time, MSRA was one of the best places in the world for computer vision, and the groups there were very selective. They had limited slots, limited mentoring bandwidth, and an undergraduate, especially one who hadn't yet shown much research output, is a real investment. You have to teach them almost everything: how to read papers, how to run experiments properly, how to write. So it's natural that the vision groups preferred PhD students or people with a track record.

At the time, of course, it felt a bit frustrating. When you're young you feel like, "I'm passionate, I've read all these papers, just give me a chance." But in hindsight, being turned away pushed me in a different direction. I ended up working with other people, exploring other areas, and that detour made my thinking a bit broader. I didn't come into vision through one very standard pipeline, and I think that turned out to be useful later. It made me less attached to whatever the dominant paradigm was at the moment.

The other lesson I took from it, and this affects how I run my own group now, is that undergraduates are often underestimated. Some of them have very fresh ideas, and they aren't burdened by knowing what "shouldn't work." So today, when an undergrad emails me, I try to remember how it felt to be on the other side. I can't take everyone either, the same constraints are real, but I try to look for signals beyond just publications: curiosity, how they think about a problem, whether they've actually tried building something themselves.

So my view now is: it was fair, it was understandable, and in a way it was a gift, because rejection at that stage forces you to figure out what you really want to do and to find your own path into the field.

r001.rationale: The response says undergraduates may lack research output and need training, but it does not attribute his growing understanding to how little he and his undergraduate peers knew at the time.

r002.rationale: It describes the training undergraduates might need, but does not present learning to conduct research as the foremost purpose of undergraduate research experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, honestly, I don't hold it against them at all. At the time it was pretty frustrating, of course. I was an undergraduate at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I really wanted to do computer vision, and MSRA was basically the place in China where that work was happening at a world-class level. But the vision groups there were, let's say, fairly selective about who they took. The intern spots mostly went to PhD students or master's students who already had publications. An undergraduate with no track record just wasn't an obvious bet.

I ended up interning in a different group, which at first felt like a consolation prize. But in hindsight that detour was probably one of the luckiest things that happened to me. I got to see how a rigorous research environment actually worked, how people formulated problems and iterated on them, before I had any fixed idea of what "the right way" to do vision was. And I think it also pushed me to be a bit more independent. When nobody is handing you the obvious project, you have to figure out what you actually find interesting.

The other thing I'd say is that I now completely understand the reluctance from the other side. I've run a lab for a while now, and taking on an undergraduate intern is a genuine investment. It costs mentorship time, and most of the time the payoff for the group is small. So it's not that they were being unfair. It's that the incentives for a research group are just not aligned with giving opportunities to people who haven't proven anything yet.

That said, I do try to do it differently myself. Some of the best students I've worked with were undergraduates who nobody would have bet on from their résumé. The signal you get from a CV at that stage is incredibly noisy. So I try to leave room for that, because I remember what it felt like to be on the other end of it.

r001.rationale: He says he now understands the reluctance because mentoring undergraduates takes time and offers the group little payoff, and because applicants lack a proven record. He does not attribute that understanding to how little he and his peers knew at the time.

r002.rationale: He describes learning how research works as a benefit of his internship, but does not present learning how to conduct research as the foremost purpose of undergraduate research experience.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I can understand it. As an undergraduate, I was eager to get involved, but enthusiasm alone doesn’t mean you’re ready to contribute to a research project. Taking on an intern also means someone has to spend time mentoring them, and the group has to consider whether there’s enough time for that investment to lead somewhere.

At the time, of course, it was disappointing. You want an opportunity to show what you can do, and it’s frustrating when you can’t get through the door. But now I’d distinguish between understanding their reluctance and thinking that undergraduate status should be a hard cutoff. People become ready for research at different stages. Ideally, you’d have a way to recognize that potential without relying entirely on someone’s degree level.

r001.rationale: It says enthusiasm alone may not mean an undergraduate is ready and mentions the mentoring investment, but it does not attribute the reluctance to how little he and his peers knew.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think it was understandable. At the time, I was disappointed—you’re an undergraduate, you’re excited about research, and you want someone to give you a chance. But from their perspective, taking on an intern is a real investment. You need someone to mentor them, and an undergraduate may leave just as they’re starting to become productive.

So I wouldn’t interpret it as a judgment of my potential. They didn’t yet have much evidence of what I could do. It also taught me something: enthusiasm matters, but you have to turn it into work that lets other people see your ability.

r001.rationale: The candidate says MSRA's hesitation was understandable because mentoring an intern takes investment and an undergraduate might leave before becoming productive. It does not attribute the reluctance to how little he or his peers knew.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions mentoring and turning enthusiasm into visible work, but does not say that learning how to conduct research is the foremost purpose of undergraduate research experience.
